category: magisterial instruction (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith)

date.note: Given at Rome on 6 August 1984, the Feast of the Transfiguration of Our Lord. Adopted at an Ordinary Meeting of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and approved by Pope John Paul II, who ordered its publication. The conventional Latin short title 'Libertatis Nuntius' is drawn from the document's opening words in Latin; the promulgated English text is headed 'Instruction on certain aspects of the Theology of Liberation'.

summary: Libertatis Nuntius (Instruction on Certain Aspects of the 'Theology of Liberation') is a 1984 instruction of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, signed by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger and approved by Pope John Paul II, that warned of the 'deviations, and risks of deviation' arising from forms of liberation theology which use 'in an insufficiently critical manner, concepts borrowed from various currents of Marxist thought', while stating that the warning should 'in no way be interpreted as a disavowal' of those responding to the 'preferential option for the poor'. It was followed in 1986 by a more positive companion instruction, Libertatis Conscientia.
description:
Libertatis Nuntius is an instruction of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF), the doctrinal office of the Roman Catholic Church, given at Rome on 6 August 1984, the Feast of the Transfiguration. Its promulgated English text is headed 'Instruction on certain aspects of the Theology of Liberation'; the conventional Latin short title 'Libertatis Nuntius' comes from the document's opening words. The text was adopted at an Ordinary Meeting of the Congregation, signed by its Prefect, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, and its Secretary, Alberto Bovone, and was 'approved at an audience granted to the undersigned Cardinal Prefect by his Holiness Pope John Paul II, who ordered its publication'.

The Instruction opens by stating its purpose: 'to draw the attention of pastors, theologians, and all the faithful to the deviations, and risks of deviation, damaging to the faith and to Christian living, that are brought about by certain forms of liberation theology which use, in an insufficiently critical manner, concepts borrowed from various currents of Marxist thought'. It at once qualifies that aim, saying that 'this warning should in no way be interpreted as a disavowal of all those who want to respond generously and with an authentic evangelical spirit to the preferential option for the poor', and it affirms the aspiration to freedom and the Church's concern for the poor as legitimate and rooted in the gospel. The document proceeds through numbered sections (I. An Inspiration; II. Expressions of This Aspiration; III. Liberation, a Christian Theme; IV. Biblical Foundations; V. The Voice of the Magisterium; VI. A New Interpretation of Christianity; VII. Marxist Analysis; VIII. Subversion of the Meaning of Truth and Violence; IX. The Theological Application of This Core; X. A New Hermeneutic; XI. Orientations).

The critique it develops is directed at what it presents as an uncritical borrowing of Marxist thought. According to the Instruction, 'atheism and the denial of the human person, his liberty and rights, are at the core of the Marxist theory', and it argues that the elements of Marxism form a whole from which the social analysis cannot be cleanly detached: as the text puts it, 'if one tries to take only one part, say, the analysis, one ends up having to accept the entire ideology', and it warns that it would be 'illusory and dangerous to ignore the intimate bond which radically unites them, and to accept elements of the Marxist analysis without recognizing its connections with the ideology'. On this basis the Instruction cautions against a theology it describes as reinterpreting the faith through the category of class struggle, and against subordinating the transcendence and gratuitousness of salvation to a this-worldly political liberation.

The Instruction is attributed here throughout to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, which speaks for the Roman Catholic magisterium. It was followed on 22 March 1986 by a companion and more positive text, the Instruction on Christian Freedom and Liberation (Libertatis Conscientia), which set out a fuller and more affirmative account of Christian freedom and liberation and stated that 'those who are oppressed by poverty are the object of a love of preference on the part of the Church'. The liberation-theology movement that these Instructions address holds, on its own account, that its use of Marxist categories is a tool of social analysis rather than an adoption of Marxist philosophy or atheism, and that salvation, while not reduced to social change, includes liberation from unjust structures. This entry records both the movement's self-understanding and the Congregation's critique as attributed positions and adjudicates neither.
editorial_notes:
This entry presents the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's 1984 Instruction on its own terms, and presents the liberation-theology movement it critiques on the movement's own terms, adjudicating neither (neutrality #1, #2, #6). Every doctrinal and critical claim is attributed to the Congregation as the document's author; the movement's self-account (Marxist analysis as a social-scientific tool, not an adoption of atheism; salvation as including but not reduced to social liberation) is stated as the movement's own position, mirroring the existing liberation-theology school entry (data/schools/christianity/liberation-theology.json), which handles the same two positions the same way. The editor does not rule the Congregation right or the movement wrong, or the reverse.

CONFIDENCE: verified-eligible. The Instruction is OPEN and official at vatican.va and was read line-by-line for this entry; the load-bearing phrases are quoted verbatim and confirmed on the page: the purpose statement on 'the deviations, and risks of deviation ... which use, in an insufficiently critical manner, concepts borrowed from various currents of Marxist thought'; the qualifier that the warning 'should in no way be interpreted as a disavowal of all those who want to respond generously and with an authentic evangelical spirit to the preferential option for the poor'; 'atheism and the denial of the human person, his liberty and rights, are at the core of the Marxist theory'; 'if one tries to take only one part, say, the analysis, one ends up having to accept the entire ideology'; the 'illusory and dangerous to ignore the intimate bond' passage; the eleven section headings; the closing formula that the Instruction was 'approved at an audience granted to the undersigned Cardinal Prefect by his Holiness Pope John Paul II, who ordered its publication'; the signatories Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (Prefect) and Alberto Bovone (Secretary); and the date, 'August 6, 1984, the Feast of the Transfiguration of Our Lord'. The vatican.va primary source is therefore rated HIGH. NOTE on the title: the Latin phrase 'Libertatis Nuntius' does NOT appear in the body of the English text on the page; it is the conventional curial short title (from the Latin incipit), and the entry says so rather than asserting the phrase appears in the document. The 1986 companion Instruction Libertatis Conscientia was also confirmed open at vatican.va and its quoted phrase ('those who are oppressed by poverty are the object of a love of preference on the part of the Church', no. 68) read directly, so that cross-reference is verified.

Sourcing triangulates three lenses per neutrality #8: (b) the primary text, the official English translation open at vatican.va, rated high (read line-by-line); (a) an academic account of the movement and its magisterial reception, Christopher Rowland (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Liberation Theology (CUP), the same academic source used in the liberation-theology entry, medium, verified to exist and on-topic, not read line-by-line for this entry; (c) the 1986 companion Instruction Libertatis Conscientia, open at vatican.va, cited for the 'followed in 1986' claim and rated high for its confirmed phrase. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. Relations: related_to and responds_to liberation-theology, which exists in the dataset (data/schools/christianity/liberation-theology.json), and which already carries an 'opposed' relation back to this entry; no dangling targets in this entry.

relations.note: The Instruction was issued precisely to respond to 'certain forms of liberation theology', warning of the deviations it attributes to an insufficiently critical use of Marxist concepts while affirming the preferential option for the poor. Recorded as the Congregation's attributed response, presented on its own terms and not adjudicated. The liberation-theology school entry exists in the dataset and carries a mirror relation back to this Instruction.

The Instruction and the movement are the two poles of a contested reception: the movement's self-account and the Congregation's critique are both recorded as attributed positions, neither adjudicated, mirroring the handling in the existing liberation-theology entry. The liberation-theology school entry exists in the dataset.

sources.citation: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. Instruction on certain aspects of the 'Theology of Liberation' (Libertatis Nuntius), 6 August 1984. Signed by Joseph Cardinal Ratzinger (Prefect) and Alberto Bovone (Secretary), approved by Pope John Paul II. Official English translation on vatican.va, read line-by-line for this entry and confirmed verbatim: the purpose statement drawing attention 'to the deviations, and risks of deviation, damaging to the faith and to Christian living, that are brought about by certain forms of liberation theology which use, in an insufficiently critical manner, concepts borrowed from various currents of Marxist thought'; 'This warning should in no way be interpreted as a disavowal of all those who want to respond generously and with an authentic evangelical spirit to the preferential option for the poor'; 'atheism and the denial of the human person, his liberty and rights, are at the core of the Marxist theory'; 'if one tries to take only one part, say, the analysis, one ends up having to accept the entire ideology'; the phrase that it is 'illusory and dangerous to ignore the intimate bond which radically unites them, and to accept elements of the Marxist analysis without recognizing its connections with the ideology'; the eleven Roman-numeral section headings (I. An Inspiration through XI. Orientations); the closing formula that it was 'approved at an audience granted to the undersigned Cardinal Prefect by his Holiness Pope John Paul II, who ordered its publication'; and the date 'August 6, 1984, the Feast of the Transfiguration of Our Lord'. Primary source. The Latin short title 'Libertatis Nuntius' does not appear in the body of the English text and is noted as the conventional curial title only.
